title: What AI Can't Do
hook: Today's AI can write a sonnet and flunk a question a child gets right. Knowing its hard edges — no real understanding, no live truth, no common sense — is what makes you good at using it.
key_points: No real understanding: it predicts language, it doesn't know what words mean.
No live knowledge: it only knows what it was trained on, up to a cutoff date.
No reliable common sense or math unless it's given tools to help.
No accountability or judgment — it can't truly take responsibility for a decision.
content_html: A useful way to respect a tool is to know where it stops working. Modern AI is genuinely dazzling at language tasks, which fools us into assuming it's competent everywhere — and then it confidently fails at something trivial. The mismatch makes sense once you remember what's under the hood. It predicts plausible language; it doesn't understand meaning. That's why it can draft a legal-sounding paragraph yet bungle a simple logic puzzle, or count the letters in a word incorrectly. There's no inner model of the world, just patterns in text.
extra_html: A few hard limits follow from that. It has no live knowledge — a model is frozen at a training cutoff, so it doesn't inherently know what happened last week unless it's been hooked up to live search. Its common sense and arithmetic are unreliable on their own; it can assert that something obviously impossible is fine, because nothing in it checks against reality. And crucially, it has no judgment or accountability: it can't weigh consequences, can't truly take responsibility, and can't care whether it's right. These aren't temporary bugs to be patched away next year — they're consequences of how the technology works. Knowing them turns you from someone who's either over-trusting or dismissive into someone who uses AI for exactly what it's good at and quietly handles the rest.

related.title: What AI Actually Is
related.hook: AI isn't a thinking robot — it's software that learns patterns from huge piles of examples, then uses them to make a good guess about something new.

related.title: How a Language Model Works
related.hook: A chatbot isn't reading and thinking — it's running the world's most sophisticated autocomplete, picking each next word from probabilities learned across billions of sentences.

related.title: When AI Makes Things Up
related.hook: AI 'hallucinations' aren't glitches — they're the technology working as designed. A model that always predicts a plausible next word will sometimes produce a plausible falsehood.

related.title: Kids Outlearn AI — and Nobody Knows Why
related.hook: A toddler masters a language from a few years of overheard chatter. A chatbot needs a large fraction of the written internet. Nobody can fully explain the gap.

flashcards.prompt: Why might a chatbot get a simple everyday question wrong?

choices.text: It predicts plausible language and lacks real understanding and common sense
It's tired and needs to recharge
It only knows advanced topics, not simple ones

flashcards.explanation_html: The model matches patterns rather than understanding meaning, so it can ace hard-sounding tasks yet stumble on basic reasoning a child handles easily.

flashcards.prompt: Why might an AI not know about something that happened last week?
flashcards.back_html: Its knowledge is frozen at a training cutoff. Unless it's been given live web access, it simply has no information about recent events.
